metals-001.question: What does the JIS steel designation “S45C” stand for?
choices: A rolled steel for general structure with a tensile strength of at least 450 MPa
A carbon steel for machine structural use with about 0.45% carbon
A cast iron with about 4.5% carbon
metals-001.explanation: In S45C, S stands for steel and C for carbon, and the number in between gives the nominal carbon content in units of 0.01%, so it is a carbon steel for machine structural use containing about 0.45% carbon (roughly 0.42–0.48%), close to AISI 1045. Its strength can be adjusted by quenching and tempering, and it is widely used for shafts and gears. In SS400 (JIS), the rolled steel for general structure, the number gives not the carbon content but the guaranteed tensile strength (at least 400 MPa), so the first choice confuses how the two designations are read. Above 2.14% carbon the material is no longer steel but cast iron, and 4.5% is the mistake of reading the number in units of 0.1%. In the hypoeutectoid range, more carbon means higher hardness and strength but lower ductility and weldability.

metals-002.question: Which correctly describes the properties of the 18%Cr-8%Ni austenitic stainless steel SUS304 (JIS; equivalent to AISI 304)?
choices: It is martensitic and hardens greatly on quenching
It is ferritic and is strongly attracted to a magnet even in the annealed condition
It has an FCC austenitic structure at room temperature, does not harden on quenching, and is nearly nonmagnetic in the annealed condition
metals-002.explanation: SUS304 contains about 8% Ni, which stabilizes austenite, so it keeps an FCC austenitic structure even at room temperature. Because it does not transform on cooling, it does not harden by quenching; it is strengthened by cold working instead. In the annealed condition it is nearly nonmagnetic, but heavy cold working converts part of it to strain-induced martensite, and it becomes attracted to a magnet. Being FCC, it shows no ductile-to-brittle transition at low temperatures and can be used for cryogenic vessels. Steels that harden on quenching are martensitic grades such as SUS410 (AISI 410), with about 13% Cr and higher carbon. Ferritic grades such as SUS430 (AISI 430) contain almost no Ni and are BCC and strongly magnetic.

metals-003.question: Which correctly pairs a copper alloy with its main alloying element?
metals-003.explanation: Brass is copper with zinc added. 70/30 brass (cartridge brass), with about 30% Zn, consists only of the FCC α phase and is very ductile, which suits deep drawing. 60/40 brass (Muntz metal), with about 40% Zn, contains the BCC β phase; it is stronger but less cold-workable. Bronze is copper with tin added; it has good castability and wear resistance and is used for bearings and castings. Cupronickel is copper with nickel added; it resists seawater and is used for heat-exchanger tubes and coins. The second and third choices swap the alloying elements of bronze and cupronickel. Because brass contains zinc, in some environments dezincification, the selective leaching of zinc alone, must be watched for.

metals-004.question: In the aluminum alloy designation “A6061-T6” (JIS; 6061-T6 in Aluminum Association notation), what treatment does “T6” indicate?
choices: Solution heat-treated and then naturally aged at room temperature
Solution heat-treated and then artificially aged
metals-004.explanation: In aluminum alloy designations, the four-digit number gives the alloy series (the 6000 series is Al-Mg-Si) and the temper designation after the hyphen gives the processing condition. T6 means solution heat-treated and quenched, then artificially aged by heating to about 150–200 °C, strengthened by fine Mg₂Si-type precipitates. Solution heat-treated and naturally aged at room temperature is T4, somewhat weaker than T6. Work hardening by cold working is designated H and is used for non-heat-treatable alloys such as the 5000 series. In addition, O means annealed (the softest condition) and F means as-fabricated. Because strength varies widely with temper even for the same alloy, drawings specify both.

metals-005.question: Which statement about the crystal structure of pure titanium is correct?
choices: It is the HCP α phase at room temperature and changes to the BCC β phase above about 882 °C
It is BCC at room temperature and changes to FCC at high temperature
It is FCC at all temperatures and does not transform
metals-005.explanation: Titanium takes the HCP α phase at room temperature and undergoes an allotropic transformation to the BCC β phase above about 882 °C. Al and O stabilize the α phase, while V and Mo stabilize the β phase, so depending on the alloying elements titanium alloys are classified as α, α+β or β alloys. The well-known Ti-6Al-4V is an α+β alloy whose strength can be adjusted by heat treatment, and it is used for aircraft parts. The second choice confuses titanium with iron, which is BCC at room temperature and changes to FCC at high temperature. Being FCC at all temperatures without transforming describes aluminum and copper. Titanium has a density of about 4.5 g/cm³, about 60% that of steel, giving it a high specific strength, and its dense surface oxide film gives it excellent corrosion resistance. The HCP α phase has few slip systems, so cold working at room temperature is not as easy as in FCC metals.

metals-006.question: Which pair of solute elements forms interstitial solid solutions in iron?
metals-006.explanation: Carbon (C) and nitrogen (N) have atomic radii much smaller than iron, so instead of replacing iron atoms on lattice sites they enter the gaps (interstitial sites) and form interstitial solid solutions. In BCC ferrite these sites distort the lattice asymmetrically, so even small amounts strengthen strongly; they also gather around dislocations and pin them, causing the distinct yield point and strain aging of mild steel. Ni, Cr, Mn and Si are close to iron in atomic size and dissolve substitutionally, replacing iron atoms on lattice sites. A rough guide for extensive substitutional solubility is that the atomic radii differ by no more than about 15%, among other conditions (the Hume-Rothery rules).

metals-007.question: Which correctly describes recovery, which occurs when a cold-worked metal is heated to a temperature too low for recrystallization?
choices: Dislocations rearrange and internal stresses fall, but hardness and strength do not drop much
New strain-free grains form and hardness drops greatly
The grains grow greatly and hardness drops greatly
metals-007.explanation: Recovery is the process in which dislocations introduced by working annihilate or rearrange into lower-energy configurations (polygonization, which forms low-angle grain boundaries). Since the total number of dislocations does not drop much, hardness and strength fall only slightly, but internal (residual) stresses are reduced, and electrical resistivity recovers well as point defects are eliminated. Stress-relief annealing, used to remove only the stresses while keeping the shape of a worked part, exploits recovery. The formation of new strain-free grains, with a large drop in dislocation density and hardness, is recrystallization, which occurs at higher temperatures. Grain enlargement is grain growth, which follows recrystallization; both are stages distinct from recovery.

metals-008.question: Which sequence of solidification structures is generally seen in the cross section of an ingot made by pouring molten metal into a mold?
choices: From the outside: columnar grains, chill grains, equiaxed grains
From the outside: equiaxed grains, columnar grains, chill grains
From the outside: chill grains, columnar grains, equiaxed grains
metals-008.explanation: When the melt touches the cold mold wall, the large undercooling nucleates many crystals at once, forming a layer of fine equiaxed chill grains at the surface. Next, grains whose orientation favors growth extend selectively in the direction opposite to heat flow toward the mold wall (inward, as heat flows outward), forming a zone of elongated columnar grains pointing toward the center. In the center the temperature gradient becomes small, and equiaxed grains with no preferred direction grow from crystal fragments drifting in the liquid. The first and second choices rearrange this order. Columnar grains have direction-dependent properties, and impurities tend to collect where columnar grains meet, so castings are sometimes inoculated or stirred to increase the equiaxed zone.

metals-009.question: A titanium alloy has a tensile strength of 950 MPa and a density of 4.43 g/cm³, and a high-strength steel has a tensile strength of 1200 MPa and a density of 7.85 g/cm³. About how many times the specific strength (tensile strength/density) of the steel is that of the titanium alloy?
metals-009.explanation: The specific strength is 950/4.43 ≈ 214 kN·m/kg for the titanium alloy and 1200/7.85 ≈ 153 kN·m/kg for the steel, so the ratio is 214/153 ≈ 1.40, about 1.4 times (MPa divided by g/cm³ becomes kN·m/kg once units are made consistent). About 0.79 times compares only the tensile strengths (950/1200), ignoring weight. About 1.8 times takes only the density ratio (7.85/4.43 ≈ 1.77), ignoring the difference in strength. For a member carrying the same load, a higher specific strength allows a lighter design, which is why aircraft structures use titanium alloys, aluminum alloys and carbon-fiber composites. Material cost and ease of fabrication must also be weighed in the choice, however.

metals-010.question: For annealed copper, the relation between true stress σ and true strain ε in the plastic region is σ = Kεⁿ with K = 530 MPa and n = 0.44. Which value is closest to the true stress at a true strain of 0.10?
metals-010.explanation: σ = 530 × 0.10^0.44. Since 0.10^0.44 = 10^(−0.44) ≈ 0.363, σ ≈ 530 × 0.363 ≈ 192 MPa. About 53 MPa forgets the exponent and uses K × ε = 530 × 0.10. About 1460 MPa substitutes the strain as the percentage 10 (530 × 10^0.44); that it exceeds the strength coefficient K is itself a sign that something is wrong. n is called the strain-hardening exponent; the larger it is, the more readily the material strengthens as it deforms and the larger the uniform elongation before necking. Under constant volume, necking can be estimated to begin when the true strain equals n (0.44 in this example). FCC copper and austenitic stainless steels are typical examples with large n.

metals-011.question: Taking the recrystallization temperature as roughly 0.4 times the melting point (in absolute temperature), which of these counts as hot working? Take the melting points as 327 °C for lead, 3422 °C for tungsten and 1538 °C for iron.
metals-011.explanation: Hot and cold working are distinguished not by whether the temperature is high or low but by whether working takes place above the recrystallization temperature. For lead the guide is 0.4 × (327 + 273) = 240 K, about −33 °C, so rolling at room temperature (25 °C) counts as hot working; recovery and recrystallization proceed during working and almost no work hardening remains. For tungsten the guide is 0.4 × 3695 ≈ 1478 K (about 1205 °C), so at 1000 °C, even though it glows red, it is cold working by this criterion (working at elevated temperatures below the recrystallization temperature is sometimes called warm working). Computing 0.4 × 3422 ≈ 1369 °C in °C is wrong. For iron the guide is 0.4 × 1811 ≈ 724 K (about 451 °C), so rolling at room temperature is cold working. Actual recrystallization temperatures vary with the amount of cold work and the purity.

metals-012.question: Chvorinov's rule gives the solidification time t of a casting in terms of the ratio of its volume V to surface area A as t = B(V/A)² (B is a constant set by the mold and metal). Under the same mold conditions, a cube casting 50 mm on a side solidified in 4.0 minutes. Which value is closest to the solidification time of a cube casting 100 mm on a side?
metals-012.explanation: For a cube of side a, V/A = a³/(6a²) = a/6, so V/A ≈ 8.3 mm for 50 mm and about 16.7 mm for 100 mm, exactly twice as large. The solidification time is proportional to the square of V/A, so t = 4.0 × 2² = 16 minutes. 8.0 minutes assumes the solidification time is proportional to size, and 32 minutes assumes it is proportional to volume and multiplies by 8. Larger castings take longer to solidify and have coarser structures. Because a riser (the feeder that supplies molten metal) cannot compensate for shrinkage cavities unless it solidifies after the casting, this rule is also the basis for designing risers with a larger V/A than the casting.
